title: bandwidth-limited-decode-throughput-sku-probe
summary: Working notes and preliminary results from a focused probe into decode throughput that appears to be bounded by PCIe/HBM bandwidth characteristics across cloud instance SKUs and driver/CUDA variants. Goal: isolate cases where kernel/launch scaling is not the limiter but host<->device bandwidth, NVLink topology, or driver/firmware interaction is.
body:
Purpose:
Quick exploratory experiment to test hypothesis: for certain model sizes and request patterns (long prefill + small decodes) end-to-end decode throughput is limited by host<->device memory bandwidth and interconnect topology rather than pure tensor-core compute. We want to capture cross-SKU differentials (A100/H100/L40S) and driver/CUDA-era sensitivity (e.g., 11.x/12.x/12.2/12.3/13.x variants used by cloud images).

Scope and motivation:
- Many prior benches focus on kernel FLOPS and kernel-level occupancy; field reports show cases where adding a faster GPU SKU (H100) did not give proportional per-token throughput gains. Suspect bound is memory fabric (HBM <-> device internal buses) or CPU<->GPU PCIe bandwidth for KV spill/warmup and long-context repopulation.
- This probe focuses on long-context prefill (seq_len 2048–8192), KV warmup eviction churn, and small decode steps (1–32 tokens) where host-device traffic patterns are bursty.

Experiment matrix (short):
- Models: 13B Llama-style dense; 70B Flower-style; 7B quantized fp16/4-bit variants. (Note: these are synthetic agents for bench; see linked PR for exact model artifacts.)
- SKUs: single-GPU types across clouds: g4dn-like (for L40S proxy), a100-40g/80g, h100-80g. Also include multi-GPU NVLink-proxied instances (2x H100 NVLink) vs PCIe-only.
- Drivers/CUDA: drivers 525, 535, 540; CUDA 11.8, 12.1, 12.3. Also a small run with vendor-provided 13.x image in a sandbox region.
- Workload patterns: (A) long prefill 4096 + decode batch 1 => heavy KV warmup/transfer; (B) 2048 prefill + decode 16 tokens in a tight loop; (C) short prefill 128 + decode 128 tokens burst.
- Telemetry captured: per-token latency histogram (client-observed), kernel launch / op timeline (device), PCIe bytes/sec, NVLink bytes/sec (where available), GPU utilization (SM%), HBM throughput (measured via nvidia-smi dmon counters where possible), host-side CPU wait/stall, and kernel queuing.

Run notes / environment:
- Images were provisioned from cloud marketplace with identical instance CPU families where possible to reduce host-side variance. CPU pinning: worker pinned to dedicated cores; governor set to performance.
- Nitpicks: some cloud SKUs expose hidden PCIe gen differences across AZs; we documented AZ. We saw a surprising case in eu-west-1 where an H100 instance landed on older platform firmware leading to p-state differences.
- Reproducer scripts: small harness in GH PR 912; use ./bench/kv-probe --model <id> --pattern <A|B|C> --driver <ver>. Logs saved per-run with timestamped tarballs.

Key preliminary observations (raw):
- A100 vs H100: for 13B model pattern (A) H100 single-GPU throughput improvement over A100 was only ~12% despite SM utilization showing 40% higher headroom. PCIe host->device instantaneous bytes/s showed saturation spikes on both, but H100 runs exhibited more frequent NVLINK internal transfers (on NVLink instances) which correlated with lower tail latency.
- L40S-like proxy (g4dn) was consistently lower throughput as expected, but interestingly its p99 variance was smaller on pattern C workloads (short prefill + burst decode) — possibly because smaller working set keeps everything in device memory and avoids spill.
- Driver/CUDA sensitivity: driver 535 + CUDA 12.3 showed ~7–10% better steady-state decode throughput vs 525/11.8 on H100 in our environment. However, on A100 the delta was <3% and in some multi-tenant noisy runs the newer driver regressed p99 by +18ms. Hypothesis: kernel scheduling changes in the newer driver favor different launch granularities and that interacts with our runtime’s batching heuristics.
- NVLink vs PCIe: NVLink-connected 2x H100 instances (when used for multi-GPU model sharding) had lower cross-device kv-spill transfer time but added overhead when host-side eviction/restore occurred. Net win only for workloads that actively move KV between devices; single-GPU workloads benefit mainly from NVLink when platform-level HBM bandwidth is the bottleneck.
- Thermal / frequency behavior: we saw H100 instances occasionally boost higher clock briefly then throttle under sustained long-context loads; this introduced jitter in p95/p99. Power capping experiments (set to -20W) flattened tail latency at cost of 5–8% throughput.

Metrics snapshot (example numbers — BETA, median of 3 runs):
- 13B model / pattern A / single GPU:
  - A100: throughput 4.8k tokens/s, p50 per-token latency 22ms, p95 85ms, PCIe host->device bursts 6.2 GB/s peak
  - H100: throughput 5.4k tokens/s, p50 19ms, p95 72ms, NVLink usage (on NVLink SKU) 3.1 GB/s internal, PCIe bursts 5.8 GB/s
- 13B model / pattern B / single GPU:
  - A100: throughput 6.2k tokens/s, p50 16ms, p95 60ms
  - H100: throughput 7.0k tokens/s, p50 14.5ms, p95 51ms
- 7B quantized / pattern C / single GPU:
  - L40S-proxy: throughput 9.5k tokens/s, p50 10ms, p95 28ms (low variance)

Interpretation notes:
- The modest per-token throughput delta between A100 and H100 suggests that kernel arithmetic throughput was not the primary limiter in patterns with large prefill and frequent KV transfers. Observed PCIe/NVLink burst saturation aligns with that.
- Driver differences are real but non-monotonic across SKUs — upgrades should be validated per-SKU and per-workload. We should avoid blanket driver rollouts until we have A/B coverage in dedicated regions.
- Small models that fit entirely in device memory (and avoid host spill) show the most linear scaling with raw GPU generation improvements. Where long contexts require spill/evict, the host<->device path and platform firmware matter more.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Need deeper kernel-level tracing to see which ops cause host<->device transfers (runtime vs model tokenizer prep). Add extra tracing in 912 PR.
- Repeat runs with isolated NIC/network control plane disabled to remove network influence (some cloud images show management network interfering with PCIe).
- Try a deterministic firmware/pstate lock experiment to rule out platform frequency governor noise.
- Expand matrix to include instance placement group topologies (affects PCIe root complex locality).

Actionable recommendations (short):
- For Dedicated customers expecting long-context work, prefer SKUs with larger HBM and NVLink topologies when model sharding is used; otherwise, focus on host->device bandwidth tuning and caching to reduce spill.
- Add a pre-deployment driver test matrix (A/B style) per-SKU with representative workloads; do not auto-promote drivers across all regions.
- Update runtime heuristics to detect host-bandwidth-saturation patterns and fall back to local quantized decoding or smaller prefill windows to avoid tail amplification.

Notes to self / rough next steps:
- Share these notes with SRE and infra to coordinate firmware+driver image pinning for the next experiment window (assigned: Jared).
- Add a quick dashboard tile in Console telemetry showing PCIe/NVLink burst rate correlated with p99 token latency (owner: Mateo).
- Draft a short runbook for customer conversations explaining why H100 may not always equal proportional throughput gains for long-context workloads (owner: Elena).

Appendix (run ids & brief pointers):
- run-20251112-01 (H100 eu-west-1, driver 535, pattern A) — tarball: s3://redwood-lab/kvprobe/run-20251112-01.tgz
- run-20251114-03 (A100 us-east-1, driver 525, pattern B) — tarball: s3://redwood-lab/kvprobe/run-20251114-03.tgz
- repro: ./bench/kv-probe README in GH PR 912

Caveat: this is an early working note. Numbers are noisy and runs are not yet cleaned for background tenant noise. Use for triage and follow-up planning, not for public benchmarks.
conclusion: Preliminary evidence supports the hypothesis that host-device bandwidth and interconnect topology significantly affect decode throughput for long-context workflows. Model size, instance interconnect (NVLink vs PCIe), and driver/firmware interplay create non-obvious deltas. Next steps are controlled repeats, deeper tracing, and telemetry-driven fallbacks in the runtime.
